examples.solution_text:
Since $13>0$, taking the square root undoes squaring.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\sqrt{13^2}\\&=13\end{aligned}$

Multiply the radicands inside one square root.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\sqrt{6}\times\sqrt{7}\\&=\sqrt{6\times7}\\&=\sqrt{42}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Write $\dfrac{\sqrt{28}}{\sqrt{7}}$ as a single square root, then evaluate.
examples.solution_text:
Divide the radicands inside one square root.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{\sqrt{28}}{\sqrt{7}}\\&=\sqrt{\dfrac{28}{7}}\\&=\sqrt{4}\\&=2\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Write $\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{10}}$ as a quotient of two surds.
examples.solution_text:
Apply the square root to both the numerator and denominator.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{10}}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Write down the values of $\sqrt{49}$, $\sqrt{100}$ and $\sqrt{4900}$. Hence show that $\sqrt{49}\times\sqrt{100}=\sqrt{4900}$.
examples.solution_text:
$\sqrt{49}=7$, $\sqrt{100}=10$ and $\sqrt{4900}=70$.
Substitute these values into the product.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\sqrt{49}\times\sqrt{100}\\&=7\times10\\&=70\\&=\sqrt{4900}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Write down the values of $\sqrt{3600}$, $\sqrt{25}$ and $\sqrt{144}$. Hence show that $\sqrt{3600}\div\sqrt{25}=\sqrt{144}$.
examples.solution_text:
$\sqrt{3600}=60$, $\sqrt{25}=5$ and $\sqrt{144}=12$.
Substitute these values into the quotient.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\sqrt{3600}\div\sqrt{25}\\&=60\div5\\&=12\\&=\sqrt{144}\end{aligned}$

coverage.summary: Authored seven examples covering every distinct assessed method, using changed values and supplied booklet methods. Questions and solutions are separate editable fields; solution prose inherits blue and continuation calculations have phantom equals gutters. These symbolic methods need no diagrams. All 26 assessment locators are mapped; accepted practice and quiz mathematics were neither changed nor re-audited. Independent example review and actual visual capture remain for the coordinator.

examples.derivation: For positive 17, squaring its principal square root gives 17. Matches the inverse relationship demonstrated at C_2 lines 166–172.
13 squared is 169, whose principal square root is 13. The stated positivity condition is correct. Matches C_2 Foundation Q1(b), lines 219–225.
The product rule gives sqrt(6 × 7) = sqrt(42). Matches the single-surd product tasks at C_2 lines 262–273.
The quotient rule gives sqrt(28/7) = sqrt(4) = 2. Joining roots and evaluating the resulting perfect square matches C_2 lines 275–286.
Both radicands are positive, so sqrt(7/10) = sqrt(7)/sqrt(10). Matches the quotient-splitting step at C_2 lines 1098–1110; rationalisation is not requested.
The three principal roots are 7, 10 and 70. Substitution gives 7 × 10 = 70 = sqrt(4900), establishing the identity by the method at C_2 lines 227–243.
The three principal roots are 60, 5 and 12. Substitution gives 60 ÷ 5 = 12 = sqrt(144), establishing the identity by the method at C_2 lines 227–243.
